content: Clinicians should always evaluate for elevated intracranial pressure (ICP), even in the absence of symptoms or signs indicative of raised ICP. It is advisable to consider performing multiple repeat lumbar punctures (LPs), such as a third LP on day 3, even if no symptoms of raised ICP are present. For individuals with an initial ICP of 25 cm H2O or higher, or those who develop or experience a recurrence of symptoms or signs of raised ICP, therapeutic lumbar punctures should be repeated as necessary. In lowand middle-income countries, patients with baseline elevated ICP or those who develop symptoms or signs of raised ICP should be prioritized for follow-up lumbar punctures. Common symptoms of raised ICP include headache, nausea (with or without vomiting), and changes in vision or hearing (e.g., double vision, blindness, or deafness). Common signs include altered mental status (ranging from confusion to lethargy to coma), papilledema, seizures, cranial nerve palsies (e.g., issues with eye movement, particularly cranial nerve VI), and other focal neurological deficits. Therapeutic lumbar puncture is defined as a procedure performed to remove cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) to reduce ICP. For individuals with persistent symptoms of raised ICP, two therapeutic LPs, spaced 12 hours apart, may be required. Daily therapeutic LPs, with CSF opening pressure measurements and drainage as needed, should be performed until symptoms resolve or the opening pressure normalizes for at least two consecutive days. If available, lumbar or ventricular shunts should only be placed if the patient has received or is receiving appropriate antifungal therapy and if therapeutic LPs have failed to control raised ICP. The use of medications such as mannitol, acetazolamide, furosemide, or steroids for managing raised ICP is not recommended due to a lack of evidence supporting improved outcomes and potential harm. No clinical trials have determined the optimal frequency or volume of CSF drainage required to improve outcomes in patients with raised ICP, nor whether clinical symptoms alone or pressure measurements should guide management. Expert consensus suggests that draining 20–30 mL of CSF during each therapeutic LP is typically sufficient to reduce ICP. In settings where manometers are unavailable, therapeutic LPs with CSF drainage may need to be performed without reliable ICP measurements. Paradoxical cryptococcal immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS) is associated with high mortality, typically occurring 3–12 weeks after initiating antiretroviral therapy (ART). Raised ICP is a common feature of cryptococcal IRIS and a significant contributor to mortality. Multiple repeat LPs may be necessary to manage this condition. Optimizing antifungal therapy and reinduction with an amphotericin B-based regimen is critical if suboptimal antifungal treatment is suspected to contribute to IRIS development. Management steps for cryptococcal IRIS include continuing ART, promptly addressing raised ICP, optimizing antifungal therapy, and considering restarting induction therapy. Corticosteroids, such as prednisolone (1 mg/kg/day) or dexamethasone at equivalent doses, may be used for at least one week or until clinical improvement, with tapering over 2–6 weeks or longer, depending on symptom response. Access to essential antifungal medications remains inadequate in many regions, with barriers including high drug costs, lack of local generic production, and limited national registration. Liposomal amphotericin B, despite being off-patent since 2016, remains significantly more expensive than amphotericin B deoxycholate in most countries. Fluconazole is widely registered and available in lowand middle-income countries, but some nations have not included it in their national essential medicines lists. Flucytosine is not widely registered or available in most lowand middle-income countries, and its standard dosing regimen (100 mg/kg/day in four divided doses) poses challenges. Efforts to improve access to antifungal medications include advocating for reduced drug prices, promoting generic production, ensuring national registration and inclusion in essential medicines lists, and developing reliable supply chains. The new 10 mg/kg liposomal amphotericin B-based induction regimen may allow earlier hospital discharge and reduced toxicity monitoring. However, very early discharge (before day seven) should only be considered for clinically stable individuals with provisions for outpatient follow-up and management of raised ICP if needed. Further research is needed to evaluate the utility of cryptococcal antigen screening at CD4 thresholds between 100 and 200 cells/mm³, the feasibility of using blood antigen titers to predict meningitis in settings where lumbar punctures are not feasible, and the safety and tolerability of intrathecal or intraventricular amphotericin B administration. Additionally, studies should focus on managing relapse or treatment non-response in public health settings, concurrent treatment of HIV-associated tuberculosis and cryptococcal meningitis, and the best approaches for treating IRIS. Research into novel antifungal agents and the prevalence of cryptococcal disease among children is also necessary. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends a package of interventions for individuals with advanced HIV disease, including cryptococcal antigen screening and antifungal treatment. These guidelines will be disseminated through web-based platforms, peer-reviewed publications, and workshops to support country-level adaptation and implementation. Regular updates will be informed by new evidence and implementation experiences.
